text: One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let's cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying on the outskirts of Gibeah, under the pomegranate tree at Migron, and the troops with him numbered about six hundred men.
Among them was Ahijah son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas son of Eli, the LORD's priest at Shiloh; he was wearing the ephod. No one knew that Jonathan had gone.

In the pass that Jonathan meant to cross to reach the Philistine outpost there was a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.

versions.text: On each side of the pass that Jonathan meant to cross to reach the Philistine outpost stood a rocky crag, one on the one side and one on the other. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.
versions.explanation: "On each side... one on the one side and one on the other" says the same thing twice, which stumbles when read aloud. Restructuring keeps the Hebrew's two crags without the redundancy.

text: One crag rose up on the north, facing Michmash, and the other on the south, facing Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let's cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will act for us, for nothing can keep the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few."
His armor-bearer answered him, "Do everything that is in your heart. Go ahead—I am with you, heart and soul."
Jonathan said, "Here is what we will do: we will cross over to those men and let them see us.
If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will climb up, for the LORD has given them into our hand. That will be our sign."
So the two of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost, and the Philistines said, "Look, the Hebrews are crawling out of the holes where they've been hiding!"

The men of the outpost called out to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, "Come up to us, and we'll teach you a lesson!" Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Climb up behind me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer came behind and finished them off.
In that first attack Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men within an area of about half an acre.
Then panic spread through the camp, the field, and all the troops. The outpost and the raiding parties trembled too; the earth shook, and it became a terror from God.
Saul's lookouts at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the multitude melting away and scattering in every direction.
Saul said to the troops with him, "Call the roll and find out who has left us." When they had counted, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.

Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here"—for at that time the ark of God was with the Israelites. [Footnote: Some ancient witnesses read "ephod" instead of "ark of God," which fits the reference to Ahijah's ephod in verse 3 and Saul's words in verse 19.]

versions.text: Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here"—for at that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.
versions.explanation: The textual variant here is significant for understanding what Saul asked the priest to do (consulting by ephod fits "Withdraw your hand" in v. 19). A brief footnote adds clarity without altering the text.

text: But while Saul was still speaking to the priest, the tumult in the Philistine camp grew louder and louder. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."
Then Saul and all his men rallied and went into the battle, and there they found the Philistines turning their swords against each other in utter confusion.
The Hebrews who had earlier been with the Philistines and had gone up with them into their camp now went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
And when all the men of Israel who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too joined the pursuit in the battle.
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the fighting moved on beyond Beth Aven.

The men of Israel were hard pressed that day, because Saul had bound the troops with an oath: "Cursed be anyone who eats food before evening, before I have taken vengeance on my enemies." So none of the troops tasted any food.
The whole army came into a forest, and there was honey on the ground.
When the men entered the forest, they saw the honey flowing, yet no one put his hand to his mouth, because they feared the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard his father bind the people with the oath. He reached out the tip of the staff in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and raised his hand to his mouth—and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the soldiers spoke up: "Your father bound the troops with a solemn oath, saying, 'Cursed be anyone who eats food today.'" And the men were exhausted.
Jonathan said, "My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes brightened when I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better it would have been if the men had eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies! Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been even greater?"
That day they struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, and the men were utterly worn out.
They pounced on the plunder, taking sheep, cattle, and calves; they slaughtered them on the ground and ate the meat with the blood still in it.
Then Saul was told, "Look, the men are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood in it." He said, "You have broken faith. Roll a large stone over to me at once."

Then Saul said, "Go among the troops and tell them, 'Each of you bring me your ox or your sheep, and slaughter it here and eat it. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood in it.'" So that night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.
Then Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar he built to the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn, and let us not leave one of them alive." "Do whatever seems best to you," they answered. But the priest said, "Let us inquire of God here."
So Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into Israel's hand?" But God did not answer him that day.
Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the army; look into it and see how this sin came about today.

versions.text: Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the army, and let us find out what sin has been committed today.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two plural imperatives addressed to the leaders ("know and see"), not a first-person cohortative ("let us find out"). Also בַּמָּה asks "how/in what way" this sin came about, not merely "what sin" was committed.

versions.text: Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the army, and find out how this sin has come about today.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two coordinated imperatives ("know and see"), an emphatic doublet that the single verb "find out" flattens. Rendering both verbs preserves the urgency of Saul's command and reads well aloud; the simple past "came about" also flows more naturally in oral reading than the perfect "has come about." The current reading is a legitimate condensation of the doublet.

text: As surely as the LORD lives, who saves Israel—even if it lies with my son Jonathan, he must die." But not one of the men said a word.
Then he said to all Israel, "You stand on one side, and I and my son Jonathan will stand on the other." "Do what seems best to you," the men replied.
Then Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, "Give a perfect answer." Jonathan and Saul were taken, and the troops went free.
Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken.
Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." So Jonathan told him, "I merely tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff in my hand. And now I must die."
Saul said, "May God deal with me, be it ever so severely, if you do not die, Jonathan."

But the men said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die—he who has brought about this great deliverance in Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he has done this today with God's help." So the men rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul broke off the pursuit of the Philistines, and the Philistines returned to their own land.

versions.text: Then Saul broke off the pursuit of the Philistines, and they withdrew to their own land.
versions.explanation: The pronoun "they" is ambiguous when read aloud—it could be heard as referring to Saul's forces. The Hebrew repeats "the Philistines" as the subject of the second clause, which also aids clarity for oral reading.

text: After Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he inflicted punishment.
He fought valiantly, struck down the Amalekites, and delivered Israel from the hands of those who had plundered them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. The name of his older daughter was Merab, and the name of the younger was Michal.
His wife's name was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army was Abner son of Ner, Saul's uncle.
Kish, Saul's father, and Ner, Abner's father, were sons of Abiel.
All the days of Saul there was bitter war with the Philistines, and whenever Saul saw a mighty or valiant man, he took him into his service.
